Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

dstask

Single binary terminal-based TODO manager with git-based sync + markdown notes per task




Dstask is a personal task tracker designed to help you focus. It is similar to [Taskwarrior](https://taskwarrior.org/) but uses git to synchronise instead of a special protocol. If you're at home in the terminal, and with solving the occasional merge conflict, then dstask is for you! https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/589d06fd-7486-46e4-b838-ce85af12f0fc [Video courtesy of xGoivo -- thanks!](https://www.reddit.com/r/taskwarrior/comments/1o7itzg/what_do_you_guys_think_about_this_taskwarrior/) ## Features - Powerful context system (automatically applies filter/tags to queries and new tasks) - **Git powered sync**/undo/resolve ([passwordstore.org](https://www.passwordstore.org/) style) which means no need to set up a sync server, and syncing between devices is easy! - Task listing won't break with long task text - `note` command -- edit a **full markdown note** for each task. **Checklists are useful here.** - `open` command -- **open URLs found in specified task** (including notes) in the browser - zsh/bash completion (including tags and projects in current context) for speed; PowerShell completion on Windows - A single statically-linked binary - import tool which can import GitHub issues or taskwarrior tasks. ## Non-features - Collaboration. This is a personal task tracker. Use another system for projects that involve multiple people. Note that it can still be beneficial to use dstask to track what you are working on in the context of a multi-person project tracked elsewhere. ## Requirements - Git - A 256-color capable terminal ## Installation 1. Copy the executable (from the [releases page][releases]) to somewhere in your PATH. - Linux/macOS: name it `dstask` and mark it executable (e.g. `/usr/local/bin/`). - Windows: use `dstask.exe` and place it in a directory on `PATH` (e.g. `%USERPROFILE%\bin`). 1. Enable shell completions: - Bash: add `source <(dstask bash-completion)` to your `.bashrc`. - Zsh: add `dstask zsh-completion > /usr/local/share/zsh/site-functions/_dstask` or source completions in your `~/.zshrc`. - PowerShell (Windows): see section "PowerShell completion" below. 1. Set up an alias in your `.bashrc`: `alias task=dstask` or `alias t=dstask` to make task management slightly faster. 1. Create or clone a `~/.dstask` git repository for the data, if you haven't already: - Linux/macOS: `mkdir ~/.dstask && git -C ~/.dstask init` - Windows: `mkdir %USERPROFILE%\.dstask && git -C %USERPROFILE%\.dstask init` ## PowerShell completion Save the completion script to a file and source it in your PowerShell profile: ```powershell dstask powershell-completion > ~\Documents\WindowsPowerShell\dstask-completion.ps1 Add-Content $PROFILE '. ~/Documents/WindowsPowerShell/dstask-completion.ps1' ``` ## Usage Run `dstask help` for usage information. ### Basic Commands - `dstask add [tags] [project:name] [priority:P0-P3]` - Add a new task - `dstask` or `dstask next` - Show next tasks to work on - `dstask start` - Start working on a task - `dstask stop` - Stop working on a task - `dstask done` - Mark a task as complete - `dstask edit` - Edit a task - `dstask note` - Edit the markdown note for a task - `dstask open` - Open URLs in task and note - `dstask show-open` - Show all open tasks - `dstask show-resolved` - Show completed tasks - `dstask show-paused` - Show paused tasks - `dstask context ` - Switch to a context (filter) - `dstask sync` - Synchronise with git remote ### Task Properties - **Priority**: P0 (highest), P1, P2 (default), P3 (lowest) - **Tags**: Add with `+tag`, remove with `-tag` - **Projects**: Set with `project:name` - **Due dates**: Set with `due:YYYY-MM-DD` - **Status**: open, active, paused, resolved ### Contexts Contexts automatically filter tasks and apply tags to new tasks: ```bash dstask context work dstask add finish report # automatically tagged with +work dstask # shows only work tasks dstask context -- # clear context ``` ### Git Sync Sync your tasks across devices using git: ```bash # Set up sync on first device cd ~/.dstask git remote add origin git push -u origin master # On other devices git clone ~/.dstask # To sync dstask sync ``` ### Templates Create task templates for recurring patterns: ```bash dstask add template +template project:meetings priority:P1 dstask add from-template ``` ## Best Practices - Create contexts for different areas of your life (work, home, etc.) to maintain focus. - Use tags liberally to categorize tasks, but avoid tag explosion. Use 3-5 tags per task at most. - Keep ta 1226 characters elided default database location is: - Linux/macOS: `~/.dstask/` - Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.dstask` It can be configured by the environment variable `DSTASK_GIT_REPO`. ## Integration of fuzzy finders Instead of passing task IDs to commands, a fuzzy finder like [*fzf*](https://github.com/junegunn/fzf) can be used to search tasks by their summary instead. This is not part of dstask itself, but can be achieved by defining a shell wrapper like this in your `.bashrc` or `.zshrc`: ```bash function dstask () { local has_double_dash subcommand if (( $# == 1 || $# == 2 )); then has_double_dash="$( [[ "$1" == "--" || "$2" == "--" ]] && echo "1" || echo "0" )" subcommand="$( [[ "$1" == "--" ]] && echo "$2" || echo "$1" )" if (( $# == 1 || has_double_dash )) && \ [[ "${subcommand}" =~ ^(done|edit|note|open|remove|start|stop)$ ]] then command dstask show-open $( (( has_double_dash )) && echo "--" ) \ | jq -r '.[] | [.id, .summary] | @tsv' \ | fzf --delimiter='\t' --nth=2 --accept-nth=1 --preview='DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 dstask {1} --' \ | xargs -n1 dstask "${subcommand}" return fi fi command dstask "$@" } ``` The wrapper function checks if dstask was called with a subcommand missing the task ID, and if so uses the `show-open` command to get a list of tasks to choose from. `--` can be used to ignore the current context for the fuzzy search. ## Database

The default database location is:

- Linux/macOS: `~/.dstask/`
- Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.dstask`

It can be configured by the environment variable `DSTASK_GIT_REPO`.

## Integration of fuzzy finders

Instead of passing task IDs to commands, a fuzzy finder like [*fzf*](https://github.com/junegunn/fzf) can be used to
search tasks by their summary instead. This is not part of dstask itself, but can be achieved by defining a shell
wrapper like this in your `.bashrc` or `.zshrc`:

```bash
function dstask () {
    local has_double_dash subcommand

    if (( $# == 1 || $# == 2 )); then
        has_double_dash="$( [[ "$1" == "--" || "$2" == "--" ]] && echo "1" || echo "0" )"
        subcommand="$( [[ "$1" == "--" ]] && echo "$2" || echo "$1" )"
        if (( $# == 1 || has_double_dash )) && \
            [[ "${subcommand}" =~ ^(done|edit|note|open|remove|start|stop)$ ]]
        then
            command dstask show-open $( (( has_double_dash )) && echo "--" ) \
                | jq -r '.[] | [.id, .summary] | @tsv' \
                | fzf --delimiter='\t' --nth=2 --accept-nth=1 --preview='DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 dstask {1} --' \
                | xargs -n1 dstask "${subcommand}"
            return
        fi
    fi

    command dstask "$@"
}
```

The wrapper function checks if dstask was called with a subcommand missing the task ID, and if so uses the `show-open`
command to get a list of tasks to choose from. `--` can be used to ignore the current context for the fuzzy search. All
other commands are passed directly to dstask.

## Alternatives

Alternatives listed must be capable of running in the terminal.

- [TaskLite](https://github.com/ad-si/TaskLite) -- The CLI task manager for power users, written in Haskell
- [Taskwarrior](https://taskwarrior.org/) -- the closest analogue

# dstask-import

usage: `dstask-import github|tw`

dstask-import is a tool to synchronize between external services or tools, and dstask.
At this point it supports importing from:

* taskwarrior
* GitHub

See below for details on each

## Taskwarrior

The import functionality is designed to aid with the transition from using taskwarrior to dstask.

Before installing dstask, you may want to export your taskwarrior database:

    task export > taskwarrior.json

After un-installing taskwarrior and installing dstask, to import the tasks to
dstask after initialising the dstask database with git:

    mkdir ~/.dstask && git -C ~/.dstask init
    dstask-import tw < taskwarrior.json

Note that the import process is lossy due to subtle differences between taskwarrior and dstask.

## GitHub

You can import issues from GitHub repositories into dstask.

### Authentication

To import from private repositories, you'll need a GitHub personal access token.
For public repositories, authentication is optional but recommended to avoid rate limits.

### Usage

To import issues from a GitHub repository:

    dstask-import github <owner>/<repo>

You can also import from multiple repositories by running the command multiple times.
# Moving from Taskwarrior

## Importing data

Please see the [dstask-import tw instructions](dstask-import.md#taskwarrior) to import taskwarrior tasks.

## Using dstask

Commands and syntax are deliberately very similar to taskwarrior. Here are the exceptions:

  * The command is (nearly) always the first argument. Eg, `task eat some add bananas` won't work, but `task add eat some bananas` will. If there's an ID, it can proceed the command but doesn't have to.
  * Priorities are added by the keywords `P0` `P1` `P2` `P3`. Lower number is more urgent. Default is `P2`. For example `task add eat some bananas P1`. The keyword can be anywhere after the command.
  * Action is always the first argument. Eg, `task eat some add bananas` won't work, but `task add eat some bananas` will.
  * Contexts are defined on-the-fly, and are added to all new tasks if set. Use `--` to ignore current context in any command.

### Contexts

Contexts automatically filter tasks and apply tags to new tasks:

```bash
dstask context work
dstask add finish report  # automatically tagged with +work
dstask                    # shows only work tasks
dstask context --          # clear context
```

### Git Sync

Sync your tasks across devices using git:

```bash
# Set up sync on first device
cd ~/.dstask
git remote add origin <your-repo-url>
git push -u origin master

# On other devices
git clone <your-repo-url> ~/.dstask

# To sync
dstask sync
```

### Templates

Create task templates for recurring patterns:

```bash
dstask add template +template project:meetings priority:P1
dstask add from-template <template-id>
```

## Best Practices

- Create contexts for different areas of your life (work, home, etc.) to maintain focus.
- Use tags liberally to categorize tasks, but avoid tag explosion. Use 3-5 tags per task at most.
- Keep task summaries brief. Use the note field for details, checklists, and context.
- Use dstask to track things you might forget, rather than everything. SNR is important. Don't track tasks for the sake of it, and don't track _ideas_. Track ideas separately.
- Spend regular time reviewing tasks. You'll probably find some you've already resolved, and many you've forgotten. The `show-unorganised` command is good for this.
- Try to work through tasks from the top of the list. Dstask sorts by priority then creation date -- the most important tasks are at the top.
- Use `start`/`stop` to mark what you're genuinely working on right now; it makes resuming work faster. Paused tasks will be slightly highlighted, so you won't lose track of them. `show-paused` helps if they start to pile up.
- Keep a [github-style check list](https://help.github.com/en/articles/about-task-lists) in the markdown note of complex or procedural tasks
- Failing to get started working? Start with the smallest task
- Record only required tasks. Track ideas separately, else your task list will grow unboundedly!
- set `DSTASK_CONTEXT` in a `.envrc` per-project repository. With direnv, this allows you to automatically switch context

# wire bash completions to dstask completion engine. Some of the workarounds for
# idiosyncrasies around separation with colons taken from /etc/bash_completion

_dstask() {
    # reconstruct COMP_WORDS to re-join separations caused by colon (which is a default separator)
    # yes, this method ends up splitting by spaces, but that's not a problem for the dstask parser
    # see http://tiswww.case.edu/php/chet/bash/FAQ
    original_args=( $(echo "${COMP_WORDS[@]}" | sed 's/ : /:/g' | sed 's/ :$/:/g') )

    # hand to dstask as canonical args
    COMPREPLY=( $(dstask _completions "${original_args[@]}") )

    # convert dstask's suggestions to remove prefix before colon so complete can understand it
    local last_arg="${original_args[-1]}"
    local colon_word=${last_arg%"${last_arg##*:}"}
    local i=${#COMPREPLY[*]}
    while [[ $((--i)) -ge 0 ]]; do
        COMPREPLY[$i]=${COMPREPLY[$i]#"$colon_word"}
    done
}

func (q Query) Merge(q2 Query) (Query, error) {
	out := q
	out.Tags = append(append([]string{}, q.Tags...), q2.Tags...)
	out.AntiTags = append(append([]string{}, q.AntiTags...), q2.AntiTags...)

	if q2.Project != "" {
		if q.Project != "" && q.Project != q2.Project {
			return q, errors.New("Could not apply q2, project conflict")
		}
		out.Project = q2.Project
	}

	if !q2.Due.IsZero() {
		if !q.Due.IsZero() && !q.Due.Equal(q2.Due) {
			return q, errors.New("Could not apply q2, date filter conflict")
		}
		out.Due = q2.Due
		out.DateFilter = q2.DateFilter
	}

	if q2.Priority != "" {
		if q.Priority != "" {
			return q, errors.New("Could not apply q2, priority conflict")
		}
		out.Priority = q2.Priority
	}

	return out, nil
}

I rewrote dstask from scratch in Go, using only the standard library, and committed it. A fresh clone runs `./compile.sh` and builds a working `./executable`.

I found the behaviour only by running the provided binary and reading the bundled docs. I didn't decompile or trace it, and I didn't use any outside source. To compare, I wrote a test harness that runs the same command sequences against both binaries and diffs stdout, stderr, exit codes, the files in the task repo and the git history. It blanks out values that change on every run, such as UUIDs, timestamps and commit hashes. It covers 22 hand-written scenarios plus several hundred randomly generated command sequences. With a fresh build all of these match, apart from the run-to-run differences listed below.

What's covered:
- **Command line:** all commands and their aliases, the argument rules (IDs, `+tag`/`-tag`, `project:`, priorities, `template:N`, `--`, `/` for notes), and every due-date form, filter and error message.
- **Task files:** they are written byte-for-byte the way the original writes them, including its quoting rules and line wrapping at 80 columns. Hand-edited files are read back, and parse errors give the same messages and line numbers.
- **IDs and state:** IDs are handed out and reused the same way, and the ID and context files are byte-identical apart from the random UUIDs.
- **Output:** JSON when output isn't a terminal and coloured tables when it is (or when `DSTASK_FAKE_PTY` is set). This includes column shrinking, truncation, wide characters, note previews, the single-task view, the week-by-week resolved view and the critical-task warning.
- **Other commands:** context handling (including the `DSTASK_CONTEXT` variable), `edit` and `note` through `$EDITOR`, the confirmation prompts, `undo`, `sync`, `git`, `open` with its URL detection, help text, version and shell completions.

Some differences come from things the original itself does randomly, so they can't match run to run:
- **Ordering:** `show-tags` and the tag part of completions come out in random order in the original. Mine always sorts them, which is also the order the original produces most often.
- **UUID-dependent results:** `modify` with no IDs walks tasks in filename order, and filenames are random UUIDs. ID numbers after `undo` or `sync` also depend on that order.

A few rare cases are approximated rather than exact:
- Unicode line-separator characters (U+2028/U+2029) inside multi-line notes don't survive a save-and-reload.
- URL detection for `open` uses a large but incomplete list of domain endings.
- Character widths for odd scripts use my own table instead of the original's library.
- A `panic: EOF` crash prints the same first line and exit code 2, but a different stack trace.

All the source is in the repository root. The test harness and scenarios I used are in `/tmp/tools` and `/tmp/tests` and are not committed.

I've rebuilt dstask (a terminal task manager that syncs through git) from scratch in Go. It matches the original byte for byte on everything I compared, apart from a few cases where the original's own output depends on random task UUIDs. It is committed in `/workspace`. `./compile.sh` builds `./executable` with only the Go standard library and no network access, and `executable` is listed in `.gitignore`. A fresh clone builds and passes the full comparison suite.

**How I checked it:** I wrote a harness that runs the same command sequences against the original and my binary. It compares stdout, stderr, exit codes, the task files in the repo and the git history. UUIDs, timestamps and commit hashes are masked before comparing. I ran about 20 targeted scenarios plus around 450 randomized command sequences, including runs inside a pseudo-terminal at many widths and heights and with fake `$EDITOR` / `xdg-open` scripts. I looked at the original only by running it and reading its docs.

**What it reproduces:**
- **Commands:** parsing of IDs, tags, projects, priorities, due dates (including relative forms like `next-mon`), templates, `--` and `/`; context handling, including the `DSTASK_CONTEXT` variable.
- **Task data:**
  - The ID assignment rules.
  - The on-disk task files in the original's exact YAML style.
  - The binary state and ID files, which are identical byte for byte.
- **Output:**
  - The JSON printed when output isn't a terminal.
  - The coloured tables with column shrinking, truncation and note previews.
  - The single-task detail view.
  - The weekly grouping in `show-resolved`.
  - The projects table.
  - Help texts, shell completions, and git's own output.
- **Interaction:** edit, note, confirmation and retry prompts.
- **Error messages:** the original's wording, including its YAML error messages with line numbers.

**Remaining differences:**
- **Random ordering:** `show-tags` and the completion list print tags in random order in the original. I always print them sorted, which is what the original prints most of the time (about 60% of runs).
- **Ordering inherited from UUIDs:**
  - `modify` with no IDs works through tasks in file-name order, and file names are random UUIDs, so the order differs between runs of either program.
  - IDs given to tasks restored by `undo` depend on the same random order.
- **Approximations that could diverge on unusual input:**
  - The URL detection behind `open` imitates the original's matching rules. It matched every case I tried except a non-Latin domain ending directly followed by a Latin letter.
  - Character widths in tables use my own Unicode tables. They matched on all the emoji and wide-script cases I tested.
- **Unhandled edge cases:**
  - Text containing the Unicode line-separator characters U+2028/U+2029 isn't read back correctly from the task files.
  - When the original crashes on an empty answer to a confirmation prompt, mine prints the same first line and exit code, but a different stack trace.
- **Date-dependent behaviour:** I could only run the original on one day (a Wednesday), so the rules for weekday and relative dates are worked out from that one day.
